t: Count Prefix and Suffix Pairs II
o: Count pairs i < j where words[i] is simultaneously a prefix and a suffix of words[j]. In "cab","ad","bad","c" the valid pairs involve "a" against three words and "aba" against "ababa", totaling 4. With up to 10^5 words and 5·10^5 total characters, the O(n²·L) pairwise startswith/endswith check is too slow in the worst case. Key observation: words[i] is a prefix and suffix of words[j] iff its length ℓ satisfies ℓ ≤ |words[j]| and the length-ℓ prefix and suffix of words[j] both equal words[i].
k: words[i] is a prefix and suffix of words[j] iff the length-ℓ prefix hash and length-ℓ suffix hash of words[j] both equal hash(words[i]), where ℓ = |words[i]|.
Bucketing earlier words by their full hash lets each position of words[j] be checked in O(1) expected time.
Explicit string verification on hash hits removes collision risk entirely.

a.i: For every pair (i, j) with i < j, directly test words[j].startsWith(words[i]) and words[j].endsWith(words[i]). Simple and correct; only viable when n is small.
s: Count the pair if words[i] is both a prefix and a suffix of words[j].
a.t: O(n² · L) — pairwise checks dominate; too slow for the largest inputs.

a.i: Process words left to right, keeping a dictionary from full-string hash to the list of earlier words with that hash. For words[j], sweep lengths ℓ = 1…|words[j]|: the bucket at hash(prefix of length ℓ) contains candidates; a candidate counts iff its length is ℓ, its hash equals the length-ℓ suffix hash, and the string checks pass.
s: Precompute prefix hashes pre[l] and suffix hashes suf[l] of the current word.
For each ℓ, look up earlier words in bucket pre[l]; count those with length ℓ, suf[ℓ] == pre[ℓ], and verified prefix/suffix equality.
Insert the current word's full hash into the dictionary and continue.
a.t: O(total length) expected — each character position triggers one hash lookup; verifications only occur on true or colliding matches.
a.sp: O(total length) for the hash buckets and per-word hash arrays.

w: In an interview, state the brute force first, then optimize with hashing (or a trie over reversed words with length-filtered counts). Pitfalls: forgetting the i < j ordering (insert after querying), confusing prefix-only matches with prefix-and-suffix matches, and integer overflow of pair counts in C++/Java (use 64-bit). Follow-ups: count pairs where words[i] is a prefix OR suffix, or answer queries online as words arrive (a trie with sorted length lists per node handles that).
